sections.content:
- Point-Set Topology (2 weeks)
The metric in Rn, open sets, closed sets, structure theorem of open set in the real line, compact sets.
- Vector-valued Functions (4 weeks)
Review on linear transformations in Rn; Continuity and differentiation of vector-valued functions; mean-value inequality, Contraction mapping
theorem, the inverse function theorem, the implicit function theorems.
- Sequences and Series of Functions (3 weeks)
Convergence of sequence, uniform convergence of series of functions; continuity, integration, and differentiation theorem for function series.
- Lebesgue Integration (4 weeks)
Lebesgue measure on the real line, Lebesgue integral; Convergence theorems.
sections.teaching:
I really enjoy Dr. KU YIN BON’s teaching style. He often uses GeoGebra to demonstrate examples, which makes the material much easier to understand. Concepts that are usually abstract become more concrete and visually clear through his explanations.

sections.teaching:
He prepared all his written lecture notes (all the content extracted from An Introduction to Analysis, by William R. Wade, 4th edition, Pearson, New Jersey, 2010.
Analysis II, by Terence Tao, Texts and Readings in Mathematics 38, Springer, 2020. ). It looks more like a review for himself to teach rather than a comprehensive lecture note for students to read. However, you have to pay attention to the content he included in the note in case you skipped his class. Because he won't include all the contents from the required chapters, especially the proofs of the theorems. Still, you have to read those chapters thoroughly using the reference books and try to finish as many practice problems as possible. He likes choosing the hardest long question for exams from the book  (not exactly the same but you can get an insight from those questions, e.g. pointwise/ continuous convergence in mid-term, taylor's theorem in final). Moreover, his mid-term covered infinite series of functions (power series) [Ch.6], infinite series of real numbers [Ch.7], Euclidean spaces [Ch.8], convergence in R^n [Ch.9], differentiation in R^n [Ch.11] from Wade's Analysis; his final covered Euclidean spaces [Ch.8], convergence in R^n [Ch.9], differentiation in R^n [Ch.11] from Wade's Analysis, Lebesgue Measure [Ch.7] from Tao's Analysis. He didn't include all the topics in the whole semester like Albert Ku did. Yet, he included 3 Lebesgue Measure long questions (all are prove type questions) out of 5 long questions. Make sure you think about the approach to prove the questions before writing. Otherwise you may receive 1-2 points out of 15 points as others did for each question (two of the Lebesgue Measure LQ are marked by xms and one of them are marked by a TA which is an easier question).

My feelings:
The arrangements are chaotic. He didn't upload the lecture notes on time because he said he's busy throughout the semester teaching many courses (I guess the best way is to read the reference books yourself as he also suggested). Besides, the homework submission is weird. The first homework of the first two chapters he taught was assigned by the end of February. We had mid-term on 15/3 (Sat) and later there were two homework assigned by the mid of April (Ch.8 due the first week of May and Ch.9&11 due the end of April). The submission date is strange for the two assignments and you better practice yourself regularly using the reference books (otherwise you have nearly two months not doing any homework/ harder questions). The forth homework (last one and ungraded) was assigned by the final exam reading week. He isn't a good teacher.

sections.content:
Ch.0 Preliminary
Basic of sets theory, Real numbers and limits,

Ch.1 Point-set Topology
Euclidean Space, Open and closed sets, Compactness, Sequence of Points in R^n.

Ch.2 Continuity and Differentiability
Continuity, Differentiability, Jacobian Matrix, Inverse function theorem, Implicit function theorem.

Ch.3 Sequence and Series of Functions
Convergence of function, Power Series, Uniform convergence and Differentiation, Uniform convergence and Integration, Abel's Limit theorem.

Ch.4 Lebesgue Integral
Lebesgue measure, Measurable function, Lebesgue Integral.

The content is quite difficult to understand since most of the time we are using R^n. and most of the theorems are written in a general form which requires more time to understand how to apply it.
sections.teaching:
3 hours lectures and 1 hour tutorial per week.

75% of the time of lecture is proving theorems.
and the remaining time is the GeoGebra classwork.

Dr. Ku will use a pencil to write down the proof in the lecture notes, sometimes he will include some graphs and examples for us to have a better understanding.

He uploads lecture videos in a very quick time （within a day）. You can skip lessons and watch videos, but GeoGebra classwork counts some parts of the grade.

The GeoGebra classwork is hard and only open during the lesson before the feedback from students. After the adjustments, the difficulty is appropriate, and we have more time (open until the next lesson) to finish the work.

The teaching speed is slow due to the classwork, and we have 3 extra lectures (This semester had fewer lectures due to holidays and extreme weather).

sections.workload:
Midterm and finals both consisted of only 4-5 problems, and usually half of them are very standard computations with many similar questions in the past papers, (e.g. inverse/implicit function theorem, or calculating some limit of integrals) so it is very easy to score around mean. Usually there will be 1 or 2 questions about proofs and those are the main deciding factor of whether you do well or not.

The workload of the course is super light, since it is just assignments and two exams. However, if you want to do well, then you might have to put in a lot more time depending on how comfortable you are with proofs.

If you have some mathematical maturity, you shouldn’t have any trouble with this course and it won’t take too much of your time (I only read the lecture notes to do the assignments and studied 1-2 days before the exams). If you’re confident in your math skills, want a challenge, and can put in a lot of time towards studying, you should try to take 3043 instead.

However, if you struggled with 2033, then you will definitely have a hard time with this course if you want to do well.

From midterm review.
(a) Given (a,b) is a solution to the equation f(x,y) = c, show that near (a,b), y can be expressed as differentiable function of x.
(b) Near (a,b), can x be expressed as differentiable function of y? Justify your answer.

(b) Proof the series of function is uniformly convergent on [a,b] (8 marks)
Use M-test
(c) Prove integral from a to b of f(x) is ... (6 marks)
* Question 5: Limsup and Liminf (new problem)
(a) Proof using Cauchy-Schwarz, triangle inequality etc (8 marks)
(b) If limsup a_n = limsup b_n = 1, prove ... (12 marks)

sections.content:
If you only aim for a B or below grade, and dun care about learning maths, then it could be a 'memorisation course' for you.

But treating it as 'memorisation course' means that u are not knowing what is real analysis, or even more serious, u dunno math ._. Maybe u are only able to do computation stuff in all math courses? Then maybe you choose the wrong major...RIP to you.

To learn better, you should not treat Maths as memorisation. Maths is about logic. Please use your logic to study all math courses...(with memorisation for doing some questions...). You will find this way help you appreciate what you are studying, as well as leading to a better grade. Then that means you are not choosing the wrong major, or at least find some meaning from your major!

For the content of Real Analysis, please find other comments.

Math is not just a piece of art (yeah I enjoy it :D like viewing the good scene and good drawing...different type of beauty :] ) but also practical... :)  If u want to go deeper properly u shd go 3043.

Kin Li is a good professor. If you have somethings that do not understands, u can talk to him. But the lecture is just reading contents in the lecture notes. (u dun hv to "take attendance"... not bad but not good. ) But sometimes he would have some elaboration more than the notes. I would say depends on whether u want to self-study or not. It can keep ur motivation for studying ge. For me, I prefer self-study everything in a short time.

The notes are quite clear. It states the motivation for the topic, and then go into the definition, and finally some related theorems. The logic flow is clear...

TO SOLVE PROBLEMS IN FINAL, u need to look for THE FINAL REVIEW to learn some tricks... since I think it is quite hard to think of them in the exam...maybe my problem.

Although proof of the theorem is not required, the tricks used are useful to learn. NOT only for this course but other math areas.

sections.content:
1. Vector-Valued Functions:
It is relatively easy compared to other 2 parts. You just need to memorize 1) how to prove differentiability of vector-valued functions and 2) inverse / implicit function theorem

2. Uniform Convergence:
The concept itself is quite hard to grasp at first, since it can be quite tricky to differentiate uniform and pointwise convergence at first. But, once you grasp the concept, you just have to memorize theorems such as M-Test and it won't be quite hard to deal with exam problems.

3. Lebesgue Measure & Integration (BOSS DIFFICULTY):
This is probably the most challenging concept I had to deal with in my entire academic history. There are many theorems and properties you have to memorize, and it's really hard to grasp the concept of "measure" (since it is really abstract) and Lebesgue integration. The finals are basically a test on this part, so... yeah. Good luck with this (you will need it).
sections.teaching: Kin Li is really great at explaining the content, despite the fact that the concepts are really hard for the students to grasp. In that sense, his teaching skills are great. He understands the intellectual level of most students in the class, and tries to teach the course from that point of view.
sections.grading: Grading, like most other math courses, is very strict and unforgiving. Don't expect a good grade on this course if you have even just a little doubt on your performance on the tests. Midterm and homeworks are quite easy while final is really really hard. In fact, since it's too hard, the score distribution is concentrated around the mean, so if you get just a little more score than the mean, you will get a much better score.
sections.workload: There is not much work to do, except for 2 homeworks (and one more optional), and two presentations (which is just explaining the solution to just one problem in tutorial session). Midterm is easy to prepare for, but final is too hard to prepare.
